def: Recursive self-improvement: a system that improves the thing that does the improving, so gains compound. In this field the term is used loosely for any agent loop that optimises inference. The strict version needs the loop to get better at optimising, not just to keep optimising.
Inferact's word for a bounded optimisation run: agents repeatedly propose a change, measure it against a target, and keep it only if the number improves. Typically 24 to 30 hours on one metric.

One long-running GPU program that executes a model's whole forward pass, instead of hundreds of small kernels launched one after another. Removes launch overhead, but is rigid: it bakes in one model shape and one chip.
A single program that runs on the GPU, such as one attention step or one matrix multiply. A forward pass is a sequence of kernel launches.
Time to first token: how long a user waits before any output appears. Dominated by prefill, so it grows with prompt length.
The first phase of serving a request: running the whole prompt through the model to build its KV cache. Compute-bound and bursty.
The second phase: generating output tokens one at a time. Bound by memory bandwidth, and steady rather than bursty.
Running prefill and decode on separate groups of machines, because the two phases stress hardware differently. The split ratio is a tuning knob that goes stale when traffic changes.

The stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed. Reusing it means a long conversation does not have to be re-read from the start on every turn. For agents, which re-send huge contexts constantly, it is most of the cost.

The long-context, multi-turn workload inside SemiAnalysis's InferenceX benchmark. It imitates coding-agent traffic: a few very long contexts mixed with many short ones. It has become the shared scoreboard for the work tracked here.
SemiAnalysis's open benchmark of accelerators and serving engines. Every data point is a public GitHub Actions run, so results can be inspected rather than taken on trust.

Service-level agreement. Here, a floor on per-user speed (for example 30 tokens per second per user) that a configuration must hold while throughput is pushed up. Throughput without an SLA is a much easier number to inflate.
Mixture of experts: a model architecture in which each token is routed to a few of many sub-networks. Which experts fire depends on the input, so benchmarks on random tokens mislead.
Programmatic Dependent Launch: a CUDA feature that lets the next kernel begin setting up before the previous one finishes. Recovers much of what a megakernel gains, without the fusion.
A way to record a fixed sequence of kernel launches once and replay it with far less per-launch overhead.
A small, fast draft model guesses several tokens ahead and the large model checks them in one pass. Speeds up decode when the guesses are usually right, which depends heavily on the workload.
Multi-token prediction: extra output heads trained into a model so it can draft its own next few tokens, removing the need for a separate draft model in speculative decoding.
Copying live production requests to a candidate system whose answers are discarded. Lets a change be judged on real workload before any user depends on it.
Time per output token during decode. The p99 version (the slowest 1% of tokens) is what users feel as stutter.
An open library of GPU kernels for LLM serving, used underneath SGLang and vLLM.
The most widely used open-source LLM serving engine. Maintained largely by Inferact, the company founded by its creators.
An open-source LLM serving engine, vLLM's main open rival. The base for both InferenceForge and Evolving Infra.
NVIDIA's production framework for distributed LLM serving. The baseline several of these papers compare against.
An academic benchmark that asks a model to rewrite PyTorch operators as faster GPU kernels and scores correctness and speed-up. Measures kernels in isolation, which is its main weakness.
NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point weight format for Blackwell-generation chips. Cuts memory roughly fourfold against 16-bit weights.
Together AI's term for re-running its agent-driven optimiser as a deployment's traffic drifts, rather than compiling once at release.
Trying many settings of existing knobs (tile sizes, thread counts) on the target machine and keeping the fastest. No new code is written; contrast with agent search.
